Importing and exporting bundles with riot

Source: vignettes/riot.qmd 
library(riot)

What riot does

{riot} (R Inputs/Outputs for Tractography) reads and writes tractography data: bundles of streamlines (3-D polylines) reconstructed by fibre-tracking algorithms applied to diffusion MRI data. It is the input/output layer of the {tractoverse} package family.

The central functions are:

  • read_bundle() — import a bundle from a file in one of the supported formats;
  • write_bundle() — export a bundle to a file.

Bundles live in R as the S7 classes streamline and bundle defined by the {fiber} package:

  • a streamline holds one fibre tract: @points is an n×3n \times 3 numeric matrix with columns X, Y, Z; @point_data is a named list of per-point scalar attributes (e.g. fractional anisotropy sampled at every point); @streamline_data is a named list of per-streamline scalars (e.g. a tract-level weight);
  • a bundle is an ordered collection of streamlines in @streamlines, plus optional bundle-level metadata in @bundle_data.

read_bundle() returns a single streamline when the file contains exactly one tract and a bundle otherwise.

Supported formats

read_bundle() reads:

Format Extension Notes
VTK legacy & XML .vtk, .vtp native, compiled in C++
medInria .fds native, compiled in C++
MRtrix .tck, .tsf native, pure R
TrackVis .trk native, hybrid R/C++
TrackVis TRX .trx via ‘DIPY’ (Python)
DIPY bundles .dpy via ‘DIPY’ (Python)
FIB .fib via ‘DIPY’ (Python)

write_bundle() writes .vtk, .vtp, and .fds natively, and .trk, .tck, .trx, .fib, and .dpy through ‘DIPY’.

The formats read or written through DIPY require a Python environment with the dipy package and a reference image (see below).

Example data

riot ships a few small example bundles in inst/extdata:

extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "riot")
list.files(extdata)
#> [1] "AF_left.tck" "CCMid.trk"   "UF_left"     "UF_left.fds" "UF_left.vtk"
#> [6] "UF_left.vtp"

Reading a bundle

The most direct way to import a bundle is read_bundle() with the path to a file:

uf_left_vtk <- read_bundle(system.file(
  "extdata",
  "UF_left.vtk",
  package = "riot"
))
#> Number of data points: 38697
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/riot/extdata/UF_left.vtk' has been successfully imported.
uf_left_vtk
#> 
#> ── Object of class `fiber::bundle()` with 2042 streamlines and [9–33] points per streamline. ──
#> 
#> • Point attributes: none
#> • Streamline attributes: none
#> • Bundle attributes: none
#>

The result is a bundle (or a streamline if the file contains a single tract). Its @streamlines slot holds one streamline per tract:

length(uf_left_vtk)
#> [1] 2042
nrow(uf_left_vtk@streamlines[[1L]]@points)
#> [1] 27

You can read any of the supported formats the same way:

uf_left_vtp <- read_bundle(system.file(
  "extdata",
  "UF_left.vtp",
  package = "riot"
))
#> Number of data points: 38697
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/riot/extdata/UF_left.vtp' has been successfully imported.
uf_left_fds <- read_bundle(system.file(
  "extdata",
  "UF_left.fds",
  package = "riot"
))
#> Number of data points: 38697
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/riot/extdata/UF_left.fds' has been successfully imported.
af_left_tck <- read_bundle(system.file(
  "extdata",
  "AF_left.tck",
  package = "riot"
))
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/riot/extdata/AF_left.tck' has been successfully imported.
cc_mid_trk <- read_bundle(system.file("extdata", "CCMid.trk", package = "riot"))
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/riot/extdata/CCMid.trk' has been successfully imported.

Attaching bundle-level metadata at import time

The bundle_data argument lets you attach a named list of metadata directly at import time. It is stored in the @bundle_data slot of the returned bundle:

uf_left_meta <- read_bundle(
  system.file("extdata", "UF_left.vtk", package = "riot"),
  bundle_data = list(subject = "sub-01", hemisphere = "left")
)
#> Number of data points: 38697
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/riot/extdata/UF_left.vtk' has been successfully imported.
uf_left_meta@bundle_data
#> $subject
#> [1] "sub-01"
#> 
#> $hemisphere
#> [1] "left"

When the file contains a single streamline, bundle_data is ignored with a warning (a streamline has no @bundle_data slot).

Formats that need a reference image

Formats read through DIPY (.trx, .fib, .dpy) do not store the image space they live in. You must pass a reference image to position the bundle correctly:

read_bundle("path/to/bundle.trx", reference_file = "path/to/reference.nii.gz")

This requires reticulate and a Python environment with the dipy package. On first use, reticulate provisions dipy automatically in an ephemeral virtual environment (reticulate >= 1.41).

Transforming a bundle

A bundle is a plain list of streamline objects, so you can use the usual list tools or the geometry helpers provided by fiber. For example, to keep only the first 10 streamlines:

small <- uf_left_vtk
small@streamlines <- small@streamlines[1:10]
length(small)
#> [1] 10

Writing a bundle

write_bundle() exports a bundle (or a single streamline) to a file. The format is chosen from the file extension:

out <- file.path(tempdir(), "UF_left_copy.vtk")
write_bundle(uf_left_vtk, out)
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> Number of arrays: 0
#> ✔ The bundle stored in `uf_left_vtk` has been successfully exported to '/tmp/RtmpMHjqHF/UF_left_copy.vtk'.

# Round-trip: read it back
uf_left_copy <- read_bundle(out)
#> Number of data points: 38697
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/tmp/RtmpMHjqHF/UF_left_copy.vtk' has been successfully imported.
all.equal(uf_left_vtk, uf_left_copy)
#> [1] TRUE

The same works for .vtp and .fds. Writing the DIPY-backed formats (.trk, .tck, .trx, .fib, .dpy) requires a reference image:

write_bundle(uf_left_vtk, "path/to/bundle.trk",
             reference_file = "path/to/reference.nii.gz")

Some formats keep additional attributes attached to streamlines or points (e.g. .trk and .trx); others (e.g. .tck and .dpy) do not.

Where to go next

  • The riot API vignette describes the package’s internal functions and the design of the C++ layer.
  • The {fiber} package provides the streamline and bundle classes.
  • The other tractoverse packages ({rtists} for visualization, {bot} for optimal transport of bundles, {toad} for atlases) build on the same data model.
